analytic.title: על יסוד פולמוסי בתורת-הנבואה של רס"ג

biblStruct.note: Within his theory of prophecy Saadya reserves a distinct status for the Holy Spirit (ruaḥ ha-qodesh): it is inferior to prophecy, which is defined as revelation of visions and sounds. The latter constitutes the message which the prophet is said to convey. Saadya defines this revelation (i.e. Scripture in its entirety) by the Arabic term waḥy. In the terminology of Muslim theologians it clearly involves sight and hearing, although some philosophers (e.g. al-Fārābī) also used it in their definitions of prophecy. Saadya's insistence on this aspect of prophecy is (according to his Introduction to the Psalms) due to the view of some people that David composed the Psalms 'of his own accord' (min tilqā' nafsih); Saadya, in contrast, believes that they are waḥy (cf. Qur'ān 10:15). Saadya's position has been explained by some scholars in the context of his polemic against the Karaites on the issue of whether the Psalms should be used as an exclusive text in prayer. This article attempts to show that Saadya's position belongs to a principal dispute over the nature of prophecy. Saadya is apparently concerned that his adversaries may think other biblical poems (including ha'azinu) are not prophecies. In the introduction to Sefer ha-Galuy, Saadya says that his rabbanite adversaries accused him of making a claim to prophethood by attributing ilhām to himself. This latter concept, meaning 'inspiration', is at the core of the dispute, and was a subject of controversy in Muslim theology. The Mu'tazila rejected it as a source of certain knowledge (like the perceptible waḥy). The Shi'ites saw inspiration as a source of the Imāms' supernatural knowledge. The Isma'ilis intentionally blurred the difference between the two sources of prophecy, maintaining that the prophet receives inspiration from the separate intelligences, while he is responsible for wording the message. Inspiration is also the source of the sciences. A similar position is found in 10th century Karaite sources. Qirqisānī vaguely mentions ilhām, while in Yefet b. 'Eli's six degrees of prophecy the Holy Spirit occupies second place. Yefet explains it as inspiration which enables the prophet to formulate poems, prayers and blessings himself, in which case he is not merely a means to convey a given text. He identifies this inspiration with 'spirit of wisdom' (e.g. Deut. 34:9), which in turn he identifies with ilhām and also with the source of sciences and crafts. Yefet's theory is an obvious deviation from the principle of audiovisual revelation, and oculd be seen as undermining the belief in prophecy. Saadya's strict definition of prophecy was intended to validate it as certain (perceptible) knowledge, defending it against those who denied its very existence or necessity. This was the first and original cause of the dispute. It is conceivable that Saadya used the same arguments in his controversy with the Karaites over the prayer.
